one_liner: Reuse the direction you were going to speed up the search.
everyday: Imagine you're walking downhill in fog so thick you can only feel the slope under your feet right now. If you took one step in a direction and it worked, your instinct is to keep going that way because the slope you felt likely continues downward for at least a few more steps. But if you change direction sharply after every single footstep based only on the steepest slope right now, you'll zigzag wildly and never pick up speed.

Momentum is that intuition. When training a neural network, we compute the steepest descent direction (the gradient) at the current weights. But instead of jumping in that direction alone, we mix it with the direction we were already heading. This builds up a 'velocity'—an accumulated direction—that carries us through rough terrain because old and new gradients combine, so random dips and bumps don't reverse your heading. We avoid getting stuck in small wiggles (local false optima) because our inertia from past steps keeps us moving forward. The model learns to trust its own momentum.

In practice, we keep a running record—a memory—of where we've been going. Each step, we keep most of that memory (usually about 90% of it), then add a fresh measurement of which way to step. Over time, the old and new directions line up, and we accelerate in the genuinely good direction. We're essentially averaging the past and present to find a smoother path down.
symbols: The momentum vector—a running memory of where we've been stepping, gets bigger when steps point the same way.
The momentum coefficient, a number between 0 and 1 that controls how much of the old memory to keep (typically 0.9 means keep 90% of the past).
The gradient, which points in the direction of steepest ascent of the loss (how wrong the model is), so we move opposite to it.
Means 'gets updated to' or 'becomes', showing that v changes on each step.

worked.title: Two steps of momentum descent with β=0.9
lines: Step 1: gradient points left at strength 1, momentum starts at 0
v ← 0.9·0 + 1 = 1  (we move 1 unit left, building momentum)
Step 2: gradient still points left at strength 0.8 (terrain flattened a bit)
v ← 0.9·1 + 0.8 = 1.7  (old motion adds up, we move 1.7 left total—faster!)

matters: Momentum shows up in nearly every modern optimizer because neural networks live in high-dimensional spaces where the loss surface is noisy—small random bumps everywhere. A naive optimizer that only looks at the current gradient gets knocked around by these bumps, taking tiny zigzag steps. Momentum smooths this out by averaging gradients over time, so the step size grows when gradients consistently point the same way and shrinks when they contradict. This means models train faster and often converge to better solutions because the noise averages out.

Papers on optimization—whether they study Adam (adaptive momentum), stochastic gradient descent variants, or constrained optimization—rely on momentum because it's the simplest way to make training stable and fast. Even papers that don't explicitly mention momentum often include it in their core algorithm. In continual learning, momentum helps models adapt to new tasks without forgetting old ones because the old gradient memory acts as a penalty (a term added to the loss to discourage sudden changes). In any setting where you're taking many small steps toward a target, momentum is the way to avoid getting stuck in the noise.
